extracted.intended_audience: researchers, peer reviewers, publishers, and readers interested in publication integrity and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and community call-to-action for detecting, reporting, and handling publications (here: a book) that contain nonexistent or unverifiable citations. Focuses on what to look for, what to report, and publisher responses (verification, retraction, labeling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiability of references
rubrics_metrics.description: References in a work must point to real, verifiable sources; publishers investigate when concerns are raised about the validity of certain references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The retraction notice stated: “Following publication concerns were raised regarding the validity of certain references. Upon further investigation, the Publisher was unable to verify the source of 25 out of 46 references in this book.” When reporting suspected fake citations, point to the specific citation(s) that appear not to be real so the publisher/journal can attempt verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion/number of unverifiable references as a reliability signal
rubrics_metrics.description: A high number or proportion of references that cannot be verified undermines confidence in the work’s reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this case the publisher found 25 out of 46 references unverifiable, and that finding contributed to the decision to retract. Count and report how many citations are unverifiable (absolute and relative) to help editors assess severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide specific citation evidence when reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports about fake citations should identify the exact citations that do not check out rather than general suspicions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The site asks tipsters to 'point to specific citations that are not real' on the reporting form. Specifics (citation text, chapter/page, URL/DOI attempted lookups, evidence of absence) accelerate publisher investigations and reduce back-and-forth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require machine-readable identifiers (DOI/ISBN/URL) for references (policy suggestion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed policy change: require that all references include DOIs, ISBNs, or URLs to improve verifiability at submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters suggested publishers require DOIs/ISBNs/URLs for all references to enable automated checks and make it harder for fabricated citations to pass initial review. This is offered as a simple, implementable step to reduce hallucinated/illusory references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake/illusory citations as a hallmark cue for LLM-generated text
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonexistent or fabricated citations are a common sign that text may have been generated by large language models (LLMs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes fake references are 'a hallmark of text generated by large language models like ChatGPT.' Use detection of illusory citations as one cue among others (not definitive proof) when assessing suspected AI-generated or fabricated content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher response and transparency (retraction and labeling practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a publisher loses confidence in a work’s reliability due to unverifiable references, they may retract the work and clearly label/mark the online content as retracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After retraction the book’s website chapters were labeled 'Retracted Chapter,' the title appended with 'Retracted Book,' and cover images watermarked. Publishers should clearly mark retracted material and provide the retraction notice explaining the reasons (e.g., unverifiable references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative threshold and editorial confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial decisions (including retraction) rest on an investigation’s findings about reliability; the presence of numerous unverifiable references can lead editors/series editors to lose confidence in a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice says 'the Series Editor and the publisher therefore no longer have confidence in the reliability of this book.' When investigating, editors document which references could not be verified and whether the author accepts or contests the findings; lack of author agreement may be noted in the notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for automated detection tools at submission/peer-review stage
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an expressed need for software that can detect hallucinated or fake citations automatically during submission or initial screening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters reported frequent encounters with fake citations during peer review and suggest automated detection at the initial submission step. Prototype work exists (e.g., attempts at detection), but implementation is nontrivial. Automated screening could flag suspect references for human follow-up.
